seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Ezra: Many thanks for your inquiry. The operation made by Vogt has certainly not failed like the others and has given him an improvement of sight. A tenth operation has to be made in Sept. You will get a full report from Zurich. We read about GA’s opera and were glad to know it was such a success. We are going to Wales for a short holiday before returning to Z. Is there any chance of seeing you or Dorothy in London.

div.note: After urgings from friends, JJ consulted the specialist Professor Alfred Vogt (1879-1943), a Swiss ophthalmologist in Zurich who was reputed to produce miraculous improvements of eyes given up for lost. JJ scheduled a consultation for April 1930, and Dr. Vogt performed surgery on his left eye in May 1930 (Ellmann, JJ 622-23).

In June 1930, Dr. Vogt wrote a report on surgery he had performed on JJ’s left eye on 15 May 1930. The operation – JJ’s ninth – had been for “tertiary cataract,” but could not be performed completely “as the vitreous body, most of which seems to have been lost during the last two operations, threatened to collapse completely by emergence or during the acute attack of Scopolamine poisoning which immediately followed the eighth operation.” Dr. Vogt decided to postpone a tenth operation until a later time. “The operation just performed will probably produce a slight amelioration of vision in the left eye,” he correctly predicted (LIII 197-98; Ellmann, JJ 622-24).

note.p: The avant-garde American composer George Antheil (1900-1959), the self-styled “bad boy of music,” premiered his modern “jazz” opera, Transatlantic, or the People’s Choice, in Frankfurt, Germany, on 25 May 1930. The plot involved Ajax, a corrupt oil magnate, who cynically tries to manipulate an American presidential candidate, Hector, who is in love with Helen, an unhappily married woman and the oil baron’s mistress. Despite embezzlement, attempted suicide, and other scandals that threaten their life together, Helen and Hector are finally reunited on the Brooklyn Bridge. “The opera ends,” the Associated Press reported, “with a triumphal parade across the bridge, skyscrapers in the background, and with the leading off to jail of the oil magnate” (“Berlin [sic] Opera Shows ‘Jazz-Mad’ America,” The Boston Globe [26 May 1930]: 6). The opera included smuggled liquor, a Prohibition raid on a night club, and the Salvation Army. Leading roles were sung by the German bass-baritone Jean Stern (1889-1974) and the German soprano Else Gentner-Fischer (1883-1943). The scenery by Ludwig Sievert (1887-1966) was startling and intriguing, and a “bizarre effect” was created by “the super-imposing of movie effects.” “Mr. Antheil had to answer 20 curtain calls at the end, though there was some whistling and booing from the gallery, too” (ibid.).

Recalling the Frankfurt premiere, Antheil noted that a stagehand pressed the wrong button during the opening scene and the enormous ocean liner that was nosing its way to center stage with the lead tenor singing from the top deck began to sink. The stagehand hastily punched the right button, and the shipwreck reversed itself with such dramatic effect that Antheil pleaded to have the error repeated in subsequent performances. He also recalled that the Austrian-American director Herbert Graf (1903-1973), being unfamiliar with contemporary American fashions, “conceived my gangsters as turtle-neck sweater boys à la the Bowery, circa 1870, although of course gangsters of our period were strictly dinner-jacket boys.” The Frankfurt production ran for only a few nights, and the opera was not performed elsewhere in Germany, because, Antheil suspected, of the growing influence of Adolf Hitler (George Antheil, Bad Boy of Music [1945; rpt. New York: Samuel French, 1990], 242-47).

Though JJ did not attend the premiere, several of his friends and acquaintances did, including Sylvia Beach, William Bird, Nancy Cunard, and Pound. Pound attended with the German anthropologist and archaeologist, Leo Frobenius (1873-1938), whose work on African tribal cultures and myths strongly influenced Pound and his long poem, The Cantos. Frobenius disliked the opera (Humphrey Carpenter, A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound [Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1988], 471; see also Susan C. Cook, “George Antheil’s Transatlantic: An American in the Weimar Republic,” The Journal of Musicology, vol. 9, no. 4 [Autumn, 1991]: 498-520).

Transatlantic received its American premiere in 1998 at the Minnesota Opera in St. Paul, with the American baritone Sherrill Milnes (b. 1935) as the villainous Ajax and the Welsh baritone Karl Daymond (1965-2017) as the hero, Hector (Michael Anthony, “Critics praise Minnesota Opera’s ‘Transatlantic,’” Star Tribune [Minneapolis, MN] [3 May 1998]: F4). For additional details regarding Antheil, Pound, and JJ’s attempt to persuade Antheil to compose an opera based on a play by Lord Byron, see JJ to Pound, 26 September 1930, notes.

div.note: After Zurich, JJ and his partner Nora Barnacle (1884-1951) spent time in London and Oxford, and then went to Llandudno, Wales, in July 1930, and did not return to Zurich until November 1930, when JJ’s ophthalmologist concluded that further surgery on his right eye should be postponed until the following spring (LIII 206-08).

Pound married the English artist Dorothy Shakespear (1886-1973) in April 1914 in London. They had been living in Rapallo, Italy, since 1924-1925. Written across the top of the present letter in what may be Pound’s hand is a note: “Am asking her to let you know when she is in London.” It is possible that Pound returned this letter to Nora with that note. Dorothy tended to spend a portion of the year in England, visiting her son Omar (1926-2010) and her mother, Olivia Shakespear (1863-1938), the close friend of Yeats.
